headline: Detours absorb ships until the chokepoints reopen

pages.title: Longer routes absorb vessel capacity
points: Red Sea security threats forced carriers round the Cape of Good Hope
Asia–Europe voyages about 10 days longer in one direction
UNCTAD: container ship demand up about 12% from rerouting
Suez ~10,000 nm, 31 days · Cape ~13,000 nm, 41 days
More vessels needed to keep the same weekly frequency

pages.title: Operational disruptions: how much capacity is lost?
points: Port congestion: 3.6M TEU, over 10% of global capacity tied up (Nov 2026)
Vessel delays: 1.7M TEU, about 5% of deep-sea capacity (Aug 2026)
Cape diversions: 5–7% of global capacity (Sep 2026)
Effective capacity falls, so overcapacity is temporarily hidden
pages.note: Nominal capacity = the whole fleet. Effective capacity = what is left after longer routes, port waiting and disruptions.

pages.title: The return has started
points: Early October: about 50% of normal container capacity through Suez again
Asia–Europe ships using Suez: 8% in the crisis, 36% in early October, about 80% before
Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk moved services back from July 2026; full return expected around Q1 2027
Suez is about 3,000 nm shorter: about 10 days less, less fuel, faster delivery

pages.title: Short term: it gets messier before it gets better
points: Bunching: Suez ships catch up with Cape ships and arrive in Europe together
Port congestion: Rotterdam, Hamburg and Antwerp have limited berths, cranes and yard space
Containers stuck in Europe: Asian exporters short of empties 8–9 weeks later
Freight rates can even spike for a while

pages.title: Medium term: the hidden overcapacity appears
points: Vessels needed = round-trip days ÷ 7 for a weekly service
Cape: 105 ÷ 7 = 15 vessels · Suez: 84 ÷ 7 = 12 vessels → 3 freed, 20% (illustrative)
Industry-wide: about 6–11% of the fleet, roughly 2.5M TEU, comes back
Stopford: ton-miles fall, the market moves to the flat part of the supply curve
Cascading: big ships move to India, Africa and Latin America trades

pages.title: Lessons from 2008–2015, and why it may not be a crash
points: Then: ships ordered in the 2004–08 boom kept arriving after demand fell in 2008
Carriers slow-steamed (about 730,000 TEU absorbed in 2009–10), laid up, scrapped and fought price wars
It ended with Hanjin's bankruptcy (2016) and mergers, incl. Hapag-Lloyd with CSAV (2014) and UASC (2017)
Now: top 5 control about 65% of capacity (53% in 2016), and security risk slows the return
The carrier's dilemma: each wants to return first, but all returning at once floods the market
